paper_title: ThinkMorph-SSL: Scaling Interleaved Multimodal Reasoning with Pretext Tasks

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: People reason with pictures as well as words. Interleaved multimodal reasoning gives models a similar way to solve problems by creating intermediate images and using them to guide further reasoning. Training models with this ability usually relies on task-specific demonstrations, which are difficult to collect. We introduce ThinkMorph-SSL, a two-stage training recipe that uses images themselves as a source of supervision. The first stage, pretext reasoning, converts visual pretext tasks, such as image colorization and denoising, into instruction-free interleaved traces. Models describe a corrupted or transformed image, generate a restored or canonical image, and interpret the result. The second stage uses automatically constructed demonstrations for question-driven instruction tuning. At the same instruction-tuning budget, models trained with pretext reasoning outperform those trained with instruction tuning alone. The full recipe improves over the base model by an average of 11.33 accuracy points across twelve benchmarks. These results show that supervision derived from images can build the visual skills needed for interleaved reasoning and improve learning from task-specific demonstrations.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: Sketching and imagery are basic forms of thinking, used for reasoning [27], ideation [81], and problem-solving [80]. Unlike language alone, they can express visuo-spatial structure directly [113]. An auxiliary line can simplify geometry proof [44]. spatial puzzle can become easier after mentally rotating an object [35, 42], and diagrams help tell stories and communicate scientific ideas. These visual representations are working states, not merely illustrations. They reorganize the problem and make later inference easier [41]. As multimodal language models mature, we increasingly ask them to solve math [24, 53], scientific [33, 90], and multimodal [25, 93, 109] tasks where people naturally rely on such intermediate visual reasoning. This motivates interleaved reasoning: creating intermediate visual representations and using them to guide subsequent language-based inference. Unified models [17, 30, 60] support this exchange natively. However, coordinating visual and language steps requires training traces where intermediate images support the question being answered. Constructing these traces involves task-specific pipelines and data review [45, 68]. ThinkMorph, for example, designs interleaved traces around four tasks, 40th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems (NeurIPS 2026). each with tailored visual manipulations [30]. These pipelines can generate more examples, but covering new tasks often requires new designs, making interleaved supervision difficult to scale. Images themselves can supply training targets for interleaved reasoning. In classical selfsupervised learning (SSL), pretext tasks such as jigsaw reconstruction [57] and image inpainting [63] use an images original structure or content as supervision. We introduce ThinkMorph-SSL, two-stage recipe illustrated in Figure 1. Stage 1, pretext reasoning, converts seven visual pretext tasks into question-free interleaved traces, hereafter called instruction-free, that train the model to read transformed image, generate restored or canonical visual state, and reason over the result (Pretext-270K). Stage 2 uses instruction tuning on question-driven traces constructed with nine automatic, task-specific pipelines (Instruct-180K). Our experiments show that instruction-free pretext practice makes subsequent instruction tuning more effective. With the tuning budget held fixed, this practice adds an average of 6.49 points in accuracy on three representative benchmarks, and its benefits generalize across unified backbones. Surprisingly, instruction-free traces still yield slightly better results than explicitly instructed ones, despite the added difficulty of inferring the task itself. Furthermore, the full two-stage recipe outperforms the baseline by 11.33 points on average across twelve benchmarks spanning three levels: basic visual perception, static spatial understanding, and mental world modeling. Improvements extend to nine benchmarks outside the instruction-tuning task families, supporting generalization to new tasks. These findings suggest that interleaved reasoning can benefit from supervision beyond task-specific demonstrations. This brings the self-supervised learning principle to interleaved multimodal reasoning: images themselves can provide training supervision, reducing the need to identify suitable tasks and design demonstrations for them.

sections.title: 2 A Two-Stage Recipe for Scaling Interleaved Reasoning
sections.content: The recipe trains unified multimodal backbone to generate and reuse visual states within single autoregressive reasoning trace. Its key design is to separate scalable, task-independent supervision from the task-specific kind. Section 2.1 formalizes the trace format, and Section 2.2 describes the two training stages, pretext reasoning and task-specific instruction tuning. Figure 1: Overview of the two training stages. Stage 1 (top) uses seven instruction-free visual pretext tasks to practice producing and reading intermediate images. Stage 2 (bottom) uses question-driven instruction tuning to teach the model to use image content to advance reasoning across basic visual perception, static spatial understanding, and mental world modeling. 2 2.1 Interleaved Reasoning Format We formulate interleaved multimodal reasoning as autoregressive generation over text and image segments. Given input x, the model generates trace = (S1, . . . , SK ), pθ(S x) = (cid:89) k=1 pθ(Sk x, S<k), where each Sk is either text segment Tk or an image segment Ik. Image segments are enclosed by <gen_image> delimiters, allowing the same model to alternate between language and image generation. Unlike text-only chain-of-thought or tool-augmented reasoning, the model itself generates intermediate visual states and conditions later reasoning on them. 2.2 Two Sources of Interleaved Supervision Both sources of supervision share the same interleaved autoregressive interface (Figure 1). In Stage 1, pretext reasoning builds task-independent traces from unlabeled images; in Stage 2, task-specific instruction tuning uses traces that connect intermediate images to questions and answers. The model thus first learns the mechanics of producing and reading visual states, then how to use them for vision-centric reasoning. Stage 1: pretext reasoning. This stage constructs instruction-free traces from corruptedclean image pairs (Figure 1, top): the input is corrupted or transformed image Ic with no instruction, not even question. The target trace is Ic T0 I0 T1, where T0 describes the visible evidence, I0 is the restored or canonical image, and T1 describes the resulting visual state. This can be factorized as pθ(T0, I0, T1 Ic) = pθ(T0 Ic)pθ(I0 Ic, T0)pθ(T1 Ic, T0, I0). We convert classical pretext tasksjigsaw, colorization, super-resolution, masked inpainting, rotation/flip recovery, denoising, and deformation recoveryinto such traces. Unlike edit-style instruction tuning, these traces do not name the operation; the model must infer the transformation from the visual input, generate the intermediate state, and interpret it. Stage 2: task-specific interleaved instruction tuning. This stage keeps the same interface but changes the goal from restoration to task solving. Each example contains an image, question, and target trace with reasoning text, one or more intermediate visual states, and final answer: (ximg, xtext) T0 I0 TK . Here, the generated image is chosen because it helps answer the question. Instruction tuning therefore teaches when to construct visual state, what state to construct, and how to use it for the final answer. These tasks progress from inspecting visible evidence to reconstructing unseen scene states. We organize them into three levels, referred to as L1, L2, and L3 throughout the paper: L1 (Basic Visual Perception) concerns directly visible content, such as objects, attributes, and local evidence. L2 (Static Spatial Understanding) concerns the spatial organization of the visible scene, including depth, layout, relative position, and counts. L3 (Mental World Modeling) requires reconstructing scene states beyond the visible input, such as alternate viewpoints and cross-view correspondences. Training objective. Both stages train the model on the same interleaved trace format, with losses applied only to the target text and image segments. The exact token-level and image-generation losses depend on the unified multimodal backbone.

sections.title: 3 Training Corpus
sections.content: We curate two datasets. Pretext-270K, used in Stage 1, is generated automatically from raw images with programmatic corruptions and contains instruction-free TextImageText traces. Instruct-180K, 3 Figure 2: Instruct-180K construction pipelines. The pipelines are grouped into three levels of vision-centric reasoning: basic visual perception, static spatial understanding, and mental world modeling. Each panel shows how one pipeline constructs the intermediate visual state used in an interleaved reasoning example, such as localized crop, reordered view, depth map, an edited object state, or synthesized viewpoint. Full details are provided in Appendix D. used in Stage 2, relies on task-specific pipelines to generate questions, intermediate visual states, and answers across basic visual perception, static spatial understanding, and mental world modeling. Both share the same text-image trace interface but differ in supervision, and Figure 8 in the Appendix summarizes their composition. 3.1 Pretext-270K: Instruction-Free Interleaved Reasoning Data The corpus contains 270,896 traces, each derived from corruptedclean image pair (Figure 1, top). It is balanced across seven programmatic transformations, including (1) Jigsaw [57]: restore scrambled patches to the original layout; (2) Colorization [114]: recover color from grayscale; (3) Super-resolution [107]: reconstruct details from low resolution; (4) Masked inpainting [63]: complete missing regions; (5) Rotation and flip recovery [26]: restore canonical orientation; (6) Denoising [82]: remove noise while preserving content; and (7) Deformation recovery [18]: undo local geometric warps. Together, these tasks cover complementary forms of visual-state recovery, from appearance restoration to spatial and structural correction. Appendix provides examples. Source images. We sample images from eight public datasets spanning natural images, web images, charts, screenshots, documents, indoor scenes, panoramas, and 3D environments: SA-1B [40], PixMo-Cap [16], VSI-590K [102], LLaVA-OneVision-1.5-Instruct-Data [2], DeepVision-103K [72], Matterport3D [9, 23], Realsee3D [47], and 360+x [10]. This diversity keeps the corpus from being tied to single image domain, and the source-agnostic pipeline accepts new image pools. Automatic construction pipeline. For each image, we apply one of the seven transformations to create corrupted input and use the original image as the clean target. We then synthesize the two text segments with strong multimodal model [58]: first captioning the clean image, then generating T0 for the corrupted view and T1 for the restored view using both images and the reference caption. Importantly, the inputs carry no instruction such as denoise this image or restore the jigsaw. The model must infer the transformation from visual evidence and autoregressive context, which keeps the corpus closer to pretraining than to image-editing instruction tuning. 3.2 Instruct-180K: Task-Specific Interleaved Reasoning Data Whereas Pretext-270K teaches the mechanics of visual states, this corpus teaches how to use them It contains 180,490 traces from nine construction pipelines, of which for downstream tasks. 62,100 target basic visual perception, 15,144 static spatial understanding, and 103,246 mental world 4 modeling. Each example includes an input image, question, reasoning text, one or more intermediate or final image segments, and an answer. Figure 8 in the Appendix shows the per-task distribution. Task coverage. Basic visual perception tasks teach the model to locate and inspect visible evidence, including visual search [93] and Jigsaw QA [89]. Static spatial tasks require organizing observed evidence into spatial structure, including spatial counting [32] and depth reasoning [25, 118] from single image. Mental world-modeling tasks require constructing new visual states beyond the original input, including birds-eye view synthesis [106], panorama [9, 10, 23, 47, 103], alternate-view rendering [67], object rotation [108, 111], and egoexo perspective transfer [29]. Task-specific pipelines. Each task family uses dedicated pipeline (Figure 2), since supervision comes from different sources. Visual search uses object-dense scenes with target regions highlighted by zooms or boxes. Jigsaw QA reuses prior pipeline [30], and counting derives gold counts from LVIS instance masks [32]. Depth reasoning uses depth annotations or estimates. Viewpoint-centered tasks rely on geometry, including yaw and field-of-view metadata for panoramas, reconstruction and rendering for birds-eye views, paired egoexo frames or 3D lifting for perspective transfer, and calibrated multi-view data for object rotation. Whenever possible, the ground-truth answers are derived from geometry, annotations, or metadata rather than being synthesized by language model. Reasoning trace synthesis and quality control. After constructing the input, intermediate visual state, and ground-truth answer, we synthesize traces in shared interleaved format. Each visual state is placed before the reasoning step that uses it, enforcing the intended causal order of first constructing or inspecting the state and then answering from it. We apply task-specific quality checks, such as yaw/FOV validation for panoramas, coverage checks for birds-eye-view renders, IoU-based deduplication for segmentation, and multi-model judging for visual search. The shared synthesis prompt further prevents premature answer leakage, requires grounded references to generated images, and disallows describing an intermediate image before it appears.

sections.content: 4.1 Setup Training. We build ThinkMorph-SSL on BAGEL-7B-MoT [17] and InternVL-U-4B [76]. Both backbones generate text and images. Stage 1 trains on Pretext-270K, and Stage 2 continues from the Stage-1 checkpoint on Instruct-180K. Both stages use the same system prompt with <gen_image> delimiter. Appendix gives the full details. Evaluation. We evaluate on twelve benchmarks at three levels: L1 basic visual perception (V [93], HR-4K, HR-8K [85], MME-RW-L [115], RealWorldQA [97]), L2 static spatial understanding (BLINK [25], CV-Bench [77], SAT [66]), and L3 mental world modeling (MMSI [103], MindCube [106], OmniSpatial [38], SpatialViz [84]). Only V, MMSI, and MindCube share source dataset or task family with Instruct-180K, so the other nine are out-of-domain. Benchmark questions and templates never appear in our training data. We score every model with VLMEvalKit [21] and use GPT-5 [58] as the LLM judge. Appendix G.2 gives the full protocol. Baselines. sections.title: 5 Related Work
sections.content: Our work connects three lines of research. First, recent unified multimodal models support both visual understanding and image generation within shared interface, using mixed-modal autoregression, diffusionor continuous-token generation, decoupled visual pathways, or modality-bridging mechanisms [11, 13, 17, 22, 39, 55, 62, 74, 78, 79, 87, 92, 96, 98, 99]. These works focus primarily on building the unified interface itself; in contrast, we study how to convert pretrained unified model into an interleaved reasoner. 9 Second, self-supervised vision pretraining has long used image-derived supervision, including rotation prediction, jigsaw puzzles, colorization, inpainting, masked image modeling, self-distillation, and imagetext alignment [5, 8, 26, 34, 57, 61, 63, 64, 100, 110, 114, 119]. These methods typically learn representations, tokenizers, or alignment spaces. Pretext reasoning instead recasts these tasks as autoregressive TextImageText traces, so the model learns to produce and consume visual states within its own reasoning trajectory. Third, interleaved multimodal reasoning has explored visual grounding for chain-of-thought, external sketchpads and tools, latent visual thoughts, supervised text-image reasoning traces, and benchmarks that expose failures in visual simulation and spatial reasoning [6, 14, 15, 37, 46, 48, 54, 56, 65, 68, 70, 71, 73, 83, 94, 95, 104, 105, 112, 117]. Zebra-CoT and ThinkMorph develop supervised interleaved traces that train models to generate and reason from intermediate images [30, 45]. Most of this work depends on task-specific supervised traces or predefined tools. We add stage before such supervision, in which traces built from unlabeled images teach the model to construct visual states and continue from them. Instruction tuning then adapts these abilities to question-driven reasoning. We provide fuller discussion in Appendix B.

sections.title: 6 Discussion and Conclusion
sections.content: We introduced ThinkMorph-SSL, two-stage recipe for scaling interleaved multimodal reasoning through self-supervised visual practice. Pretext-270K provides instruction-free traces for producing and interpreting intermediate images, while Instruct-180K supplies automatically constructed demonstrations for question-driven instruction tuning. Pretext training improves subsequent learning at fixed instruction-tuning budget, and the full recipe improves performance across perception, spatial understanding, and mental world modeling. These findings show that supervision need not be designed around downstream questions to benefit interleaved reasoning. Images themselves can provide scalable training targets that make learning from task-specific demonstrations more effective. Limitations. Our pretext pipeline constructs supervision automatically, but we have not systematically measured how performance changes with more pretext data, training compute, or larger models. We study seven visual pretext tasks and evaluate mainly perception and spatial reasoning; whether the recipe extends to other tasks and domains remains open. Interleaved reasoning also has substantial inference costs, which may limit its use when compute or latency is constrained. Finally, the base models pretraining data are not public, so overlap with our source data cannot be ruled out. Broader impact. We openly release the datasets, model checkpoints, and code to support research on interleaved multimodal reasoning. Better spatial reasoning could help assistive systems describe scenes and explain layouts. The model may also reproduce biases in its pretrained backbone and the public datasets used here; we have not audited those biases.

sections.title: A Overview of the Appendix
sections.content: This appendix is organized as follows: Section extends the related-work discussion. Section reports the composition of Pretext-270K and Instruct-180K. Section details the task-specific Instruct-180K pipelines and the shared trace synthesis prompt. Section shows example traces per Instruct-180K task, and Section shows one Text ImageText trace per pretext task. Section reports training and evaluation details: hyperparameters of the main and ablation runs, the loss, system prompts, compute, the VLMEvalKit configuration, per-benchmark scoring, and judge prompts. Section presents qualitative good cases and failure modes of ThinkMorph-SSL, data overlap, and alternative routes without visual-state training.

sections.title: B Extended Related Work
sections.content: Unified multimodal models. Recent unified multimodal models support visual understanding and image generation within shared interface. Existing approaches vary in how they connect the two capabilities, from early-fusion mixed-modal modeling [74] to autoregressive token-based unification [87, 96, 98, 99] and continuous-token or diffusion-based variants [11, 22]; another line decouples or harmonizes visual pathways [13, 55, 92] or introduces latent or query-based bridges between modalities [39, 62], and complementary line studies adaptationor pretraining-based recipes [78, 79]. We build on BAGEL, which shows that large-scale interleaved pretraining can yield emergent unified capabilities [17]. These works primarily address how to build or adapt the unified interface itself. In contrast, ThinkMorph-SSL studies the orthogonal training bridge from generic unified competence to interleaved reasoning behavior: pretext reasoning is inserted between unified pretraining and question-driven instruction tuning to teach the model the mechanics of TextImageText continuation before supervised reasoning. Self-supervised visual pretraining. long line of work learns visual representations without human labels by constructing supervision from the image itself. Early pretext tasks include instance and rotation discrimination [19, 26], spatial-context and jigsaw puzzles [18, 57], color and inpainting reconstructions [63, 114], and motion-based signals from video [1, 86]. These ideas later scaled through masked image modeling [5, 34, 100, 119], self-distillation [8, 61], and imagetext alignment [64, 110]. Despite their diversity, these objectives primarily produce an encoder, tokenizer, or an alignment space; the model is not trained to use visual generation as part of its own computation. Pretext reasoning revisits this paradigm but changes the interface: each restoration task is reformulated as an autoregressive TextImageText trace. The resulting supervision trains unified model to continue interleaved perception and generation trajectories rather than merely produce visual representation. Interleaved multimodal reasoning. Cognitive science has long argued that human spatial reasoning often relies on mental imagery and visual simulation rather than purely verbal deduction [43, 69]. This motivates models that can reason through intermediate visual states instead of expressing every step only in text. Prior work brings visual content into reasoning in three main ways. The first augments textual chain-of-thought with visual grounding [15, 68, 94] or with external programmatic[20], agentstyle, and sketchpad tools [37, 73, 105]; recent work further trains models to invoke vision specialists or pixel-space operations adaptively [56, 70, 71], often through reinforcement learning over images [59, 83, 117, 121]. These methods improve evidence gathering and interpretability, but the reasoning trace remains primarily textual or tool-mediated, and its visual operations are bounded by predefined tools or experts. The second line incorporates visual state directly into the reasoning trajectory. Some methods train on supervised interleaved text-image reasoning traces [14, 30, 45]; others introduce latent visual tokens as task-specific intermediates, mental imagery, internal sketchpads, or modality-agnostic thought tokens 20 Figure 8: Corpus composition. Left: traces per pretext transformation in Pretext-270K. Right: traces in Instruct-180K per level (inner ring; L1 basic visual perception, L2 static spatial understanding, L3 mental world modeling) and per construction pipeline (outer ring; nine pipelines). [6, 65, 104, 112]. Complementary work studies test-time scaling and representation bottlenecks for such multimodal reasoning processes [12, 39]. Recent benchmarks further motivate this direction, showing that current models struggle when answers depend on intermediate visual states, visual simulation, or causal-spatial structure rather than language-only reasoning [46, 48, 54, 95, 120]. The third line studies interleaved multimodal generation, where mixed image-text content is the final artifact rather than an intermediate reasoning process [31, 49, 50, 101]. This direction is complementary to our goal, since we use generated visual states as intermediate thoughts to improve multimodal understanding and reasoning. Across these lines, the dominant recipe relies on supervised reasoning traces, which are costly to scale and limited in coverage. We target the stage that prior work largely skips. Pretext reasoning provides instruction-free training, before any question-driven supervision, that teaches unified model the mechanics of TextImageText continuation, while Instruct-180K then fits within the supervised interleaved-reasoning lineage as question-driven corpus.

sections.title: C Data Composition
sections.content: Figure 8 shows the composition of both corpora. Pretext-270K draws its images from SA-1B, PixMo-Cap, VSI-590K, LLaVA-OneVision-1.5-Instruct-Data, and DeepVision-103K for all seven transformations, and additionally from Realsee3D, 360+x, and Matterport3D for Jigsaw. Implementation Details of the Instruct-180K Curation Pipeline Table 6 maps each level of Instruct-180K to its task families and to the kind of intermediate image its traces construct. Table 6: Role of the intermediate visual state at each level of Instruct-180K. Level Role of the visual state Task families Intermediate image L1: Basic visual perception Focus on visible evidence Visual search, Jigsaw QA L2: Static spatial understanding L3: Mental world modeling Organize visible spatial relations Reconstruct unseen or transformed states Spatial counting, depth reasoning Birds-eye view synthesis, panorama, alternate-view rendering, object rotation, egoexo perspective transfer Target boxed or zoomed in the scene; unscrambled image Instance crops; depth map Birds-eye view; panorama; alternate view; rotated object; another agents view Mental world modeling further splits into viewpoint synthesis, where the camera moves while the scene stays fixed, and object manipulation, where the camera stays while the object changes. Within viewpoint synthesis the subsections are ordered by how far the synthesized view departs from the input egocentric frame. Panorama stays at the same camera position with wider field of view. Birds-eye view synthesis leaves the agent for world-anchored overhead. Egoexo perspective transfer and alternate-view rendering both adopt another entitys viewpoint; the first learns from real paired ego/exo captures and the second from single-image 3D lifts, since no single source covers both. D.1 Interleaved chain-of-thought generation Each row arrives with the question stem, the gold label, input images, and zero or more reasoning images that have already been rendered or photographed. separate vision-language pass writes the trace student model is trained to mimic. For attached reasoning images the writer returns + 1 text blocks alternating with those images. The first block is written before any generated view is consulted: it inspects the inputs, states what visualization will come next, and explains why. Each later block is written after its corresponding image: it describes what that view makes explicit, ties it back to the inputs, and either plans the next view or concludes. The writer is invoked through two cascaded prompts. An optional first pass paraphrases the question and answer to diversify surface form without changing semantics. The main pass casts the model as an agent that generates the intermediate views during reasoning, under three constraints: it must not refer to the views as externally supplied, it must not leak the gold answer before the final block, and it must use descriptive view names (birds-eye view, depth map) rather than ordinal labels. The model sees the stem, the answer, per-task suggested reasoning approach, and the input and reasoning images in alternation. When per-row metadata indicates which reasoning view corresponds to which input, that correspondence is attached as hidden hint usable only for internal consistency. Outputs that omit any of the + 1 expected blocks are rejected and re-run. Tasks that do not commit to visual reasoning sequence skip reasoning images. The model returns single continuous-prose chain under lighter system prompt that forbids bullet inventories and mechanical enumeration. Per-task templates supply both the suggested reasoning approach and the short captions used to label the attached reasoning images. The fixed system roles below are shared across tasks. The template excerpts that follow are representative rather than exhaustive. REWRITE_SYSTEM_PROMPT (optional questionanswer paraphrase). Rewrite the given question and answer with diverse wording and sentence structure while preserving correctness. Rules: 1. Preserve the original meaning -- do not alter spatial relations, change counts, swap entities, or introduce ambiguity. All entities, constraints, and spatial details must be retained. 2. Vary vocabulary, sentence structure, and phrasing style freely. Do not add hints toward the answer. 3. For multiple-choice questions, keep the option order unchanged; you may rephrase option text if the meaning is preserved. 4. Output JSON object with keys: "question", "answer". CORE_SYSTEM_PROMPT (interleaved reasoning images). You are an advanced spatial reasoning AI with unique capability: you can generate intermediate visualizations (e.g., birds-eye views, side profiles, depth maps, rotated perspectives, or step-by-step constructions) to help understand spatial relationships. Your Task: You will be given: 1. Input Images: One or more images related to the task (e.g., multiple viewpoints of scene, puzzle layout, diagram, etc.). 2. Intermediate Generated Views: sequence of visual aids you "generate" during reasoning (e.g., new perspectives, step-by-step 22 assembly stages, annotated overlays, etc.). 3. spatial reasoning question and its correct answer. Your Goal: Generate textual reasoning that connects these images step-by-step. Since you have the capability to "generate" these intermediate views, you must explain why you need them and what they show. For intermediate views, you need N+1 reasoning blocks: * reasoning_thought_0: BEFORE generating any view - Analyze the initial Input Images and questions. - Explicitly state what type of view you will generate next and why. * reasoning_thought_1: AFTER generating the first view - Now you can see the generated image. - Describe the type of view you generated (e.g., "This top-down perspective reveals...") and analyze its content. - Synthesize this with the original inputs. - State what you will generate next (if needed). * reasoning_thought_2: AFTER generating the second view - Describe the new view and what information it provides. - Synthesize all observations to derive the final answer. * (Continue this pattern for more views if needed.) Output Format: Return your reasoning as JSON object with the required keys. Important Notes: 1. Never describe view before generating it. In reasoning_thought_0 you only state your intention to generate specific type of view. 2. Dynamic Terminology: Do not use generic labels like "Image 1". Instead, use descriptive terms based on the view type, such as "the birds-eye view", "the depth map", "the side-angle perspective", or "the zoomed-in visualization". 3. Cross-Referencing: Intermediate views help with structure but may lack specific details. If you need, please refer back to the Input Images for fine-grained object identification. 4. Step-by-Step Deduction: Your conclusion must be the logical result of combining the input images with your generated visualizations. 5. Do not state, hint at, or assume the correct answer in the reasoning process. Do not refer to intermediate views as "provided" or "given"; describe them as views you generate during reasoning. TEXT_ONLY_SYSTEM_PROMPT (no intermediate images). You are an advanced spatial reasoning AI. Your Task: You will be given: 1. Input Images: One or more images related to the task. 2. spatial reasoning question and its correct answer. Your Goal: Generate natural chain-of-thought reasoning that explains how to arrive at the correct answer by analyzing the input images. Output Format: Return your reasoning as JSON object with exactly one 23 key: "reasoning". Important Notes: 1. Think naturally. Write your reasoning as continuous, flowing thought process -- as if you are talking through the problem. Avoid rigid numbered lists, bullet-by-bullet image inventories, or mechanical enumeration patterns like "Count = 1, Count = 2". 2. Build toward the answer progressively. Do not state or assume the correct answer at the beginning. Let your conclusion emerge from your observations and spatial analysis. Counting with mask overlay (lvis_mask_counting). Task: Count how many instances of the queried object category are in the image. reasoning_thought_0 (BEFORE generating any view): Observe the input image, identify the queried object category, and note any challenges for counting (occlusion, clutter, similar-looking objects). Explain why you will generate mask overlay that isolates only the target instances on white background. reasoning_thought_1 (AFTER generating the mask overlay): The generated mask overlay shows only the target instances on white background with black contours around each instance. Count each distinct instance visible in the overlay carefully and state the final count. Top-down counting on multi-view scenes (topdown_counting). Task: Count how many instances of the queried object category are in the full scene. reasoning_thought_0: Briefly inspect the multi-view input images, and explain why you will generate top-down view. reasoning_thought_1: Describe what the generated top-down view reveals, count the queried category carefully in that view, and finish with the final count consistent with the question. RefSpatial depth with two generated views (refspatial_point_depth). Task: Answer RefSpatial depth question using the available generated depth-support view or views. When there are two generated views, use the first to localize the correct point or points and the second to make the final depth judgment. For reasoning_thought_0, briefly inspect the input image and question, explain what depth relation must be resolved, and state what kind of depth-support view you will form next. Do not answer yet. Egoexo perspective transfer (egoexo_perspective_taking). Task: Answer perspective-taking spatial question from third-person scene image. The input image shows the scene from an outside view, while the generated view represents the queried persons first-person perspective. Do not mention raw field names such as images, reasoning_image_0, or any hidden metadata. Do not mention markers, highlights, or annotations that are not visible to the final solver. Instead, refer naturally to the outside scene view and the generated first-person view. 24 reasoning_thought_0 (BEFORE generating any view): Inspect the third-person image, identify which person the question refers to, locate the relevant object or objects mentioned in the question, and explain why the answer cannot be judged directly from the outside camera. State that you will generate first-person view from that persons position and facing direction so the relation can be judged from their own perspective. Do not reveal the final answer yet. reasoning_thought_1 (AFTER generating the first view): Analyze the generated first-person view from that persons perspective. Use it to determine the asked relation precisely, such as left versus right, above versus below, or front versus behind. Keep the reasoning grounded in visible scene evidence and perspective transformation only, then finish with the correct answer. Panorama merge (panorama_spatial). Task: Answer spatial reasoning question about an indoor or outdoor scene captured from two partially overlapping viewpoints (left view and right view from the same camera position). The merged panoramic view provides wider field of view that reveals the full spatial layout. reasoning_thought_0 (BEFORE generating any view): Inspect the two input images carefully. Identify the key objects, scene areas, and spatial cues mentioned in the question. Note how the two views overlap at the center (shared region) and what each view uniquely shows on its periphery. Explain that you will generate merged panoramic view to see the complete spatial layout and resolve the relationship asked. Do not answer yet. reasoning_thought_1 (AFTER generating the merged view): Analyze the generated merged panoramic view. Use it to determine the full spatial layout -- identify where objects and scene areas are located relative to each other and relative to the camera. Cross-reference with the original input images for fine-grained object identification. Derive the final answer through step-by-step spatial reasoning grounded in the visual evidence. Mindcube-style left/right with two top-downs (template_02_directional_query). Task: Answer left/right query for the target object from one queried input viewpoint. Do not mention raw field names such as reasoning_image_0, reasoning_image_1, prompt_metadata, or reasoning_image_1_matches_image_index in the output reasoning. Do not mention any hidden hint, metadata, annotation, field name, or externally provided correspondence in the output reasoning. Instead, refer to the visual evidence naturally as the first generated top-down view, the rotated top-down view, or the corresponding original image. reasoning_thought_0 (BEFORE generating any view): Inspect the queried input image and the other input images briefly. State that you will first form birds-eye view of the queried viewpoint, which helps convert the egocentric left/right question into rotation on the top-down layout. Do not answer yet. reasoning_thought_1 (AFTER generating the first view): Analyze that first birds-eye view, then apply the 90-degree rotation rule 25 (clockwise for left questions, anticlockwise for right questions in this dataset) to explain why you need the second generated view. Keep this step focused on forming the rotated view itself, without yet naming which original image it matches. reasoning_thought_2 (AFTER generating the second view): State which original input image has the same orientation as the rotated view, then use that matched original input image to identify what lies in front in the aligned view, because that matched original image is the normal-perspective version of the rotated view. So the actual object judgment should be made from the matched original input image, then translated back into the answer for the queried viewpoint. Use the original images to confirm object identity and appearance details, and keep the explanation grounded in visual reasoning only. Downstream, modality-specific post-filters (for example the panorama CoT consistency check in Section D.4.1) assume these fields are already present on each row. D.2 Basic visual perception D.2.1 Visual search Visual search targets single object inside an object-dense scene. Images must contain at least 135 annotated bounding boxes to ensure sufficient object density for unambiguous target selection. For each candidate target, templated GPT call conditioned on the full image with red bounding box drawn around the target or high-resolution crop of that object generates four-option multiple-choice question spanning fine-grained attribute recognition, spatial relationships, OCR, and visual reasoning. The correct answer must be verifiable from the cropped view alone, so the intermediate imagethe full scene with the red bounding box renderedis by construction the visual artifact required to answer. four-model judge ensemble (GPT-4.1, Gemini-2.5 Pro, GPT-5.1, and Gemini-3-ProPreview) then rejects items on any of four failure criteria: visual mismatch or ambiguity (VIS_FAIL), poor question logic (LOGIC_FAIL), incorrect ground-truth answer (ANS_ERR), or absence of visual evidence in the crop (NO_EVID). D.3 Static spatial understanding D.3.1 Spatial counting Object-counting supervision is sampled from LVIS [32], which provides high-quality instance segmentation masks for large open vocabulary. For each image we enumerate instances whose mask area clears minimum pixel threshold, crop each instance with small margin from its axis-aligned box, and pair the crops with questions whose gold counts come from the mask inventory alone, with no language-model labelling of the number. The task tests whether the model can aggregate fragmented visual evidence into verifiable count. D.3.2 Depth reasoning Depth-oriented questions are subsampled from the RefSpatial corpus introduced in RoboRefer [118], whose annotations include depth-related probes. We keep the original question and answer semantics but replace the depth or disparity visualization: scalar maps are re-coloured with the viridis colormap for perceptual uniformity and clearer contrast in printed traces, without changing the underlying geometry. D.4 Mental world modeling D.4.1 Viewpoint synthesis Panorama. The smallest departure from the input is to stay at the same camera position and widen the field of view. Supervision for this comes from equirectangular panoramas (Matterport3D [9, 23], RealSee-3D [47], 360+x [10] scans). Because we can synthesize pairs of perspective crops at 26 controlled yaw, pitch, and field of view, the yaw separation between the two views is known exactly, which lets us derive ground-truth answers for many spatial questions analytically rather than asking vision-language model to read them off pixels. Each panorama becomes stream of multiple-choice questions whose images are two perspective crops and whose reasoning aid is the side-by-side composite of those crops. We synthesize two question families on the same view-extraction frontend, distinguished by who decides the answer. template-driven family covers cases where view metadata does not pin down the answer (compass premises, measurement, object identification, scene navigation, camera motion); vision-language model writes the question and picks the gold option, gated by metadataconsistency checks on the subset where geometry is verifiable. For the geometric subset where metadata determines the answer, we use an analytical generation pipeline: the model only names objects and writes prose around an analytically fixed direction. The pipeline runs in four stages. Step 1: Perspective view extraction. For each panorama we sample base pair (left, right) sharing the camera position but offset in yaw. Per-view FOV is drawn from (60, 90), the desired angular overlap from (5, 50) (negative values indicate gap), and small pitch jitter from (5, 5). The yaw separation that realizes the requested overlap is yawsep = max (cid:16) 0, 1 (cid:17) 2 (fovL + fovR) overlap , placed symmetrically about the panoramas reference yaw. Each crop is rendered by direct equirectangular-to-perspective resampling: pixels are lifted to camera-frame rays, rotated by the requested yaw and pitch, converted back to spherical coordinates, and bilinearly sampled from the panorama. No distortion model is needed because the source is already rectified to equirectangular convention. To support multi-image mental spatial reasoning and cannot-be-determined questions, we extend each scene with additional crops on both sides of the base pair. From each base view, we sample chain of crops with random yaw offsets, stopping when candidate overlaps with the opposite base view above small threshold. The resulting auxiliary views tile the half-sphere away from the base pair without re-entering it. We save the side-by-side composite of the left and right chains as the reasoning-aid image attached to every question for the scene. Step 2: Question synthesis. The template catalog covers photographer-relative directions, compass premises, objectobject relations, camera motion (translation and rotation), measurement, and object identification, plus reserved cannot-be-determined category for non-overlapping pairs. Templates are sampled per scene with category-specific weights. The regeneration shares the per-scene RNG seeding, so its output concatenates with the main pass without overlap. Step 3: Verification. Every candidate clears four cumulative gates before it is written. The forbidden-leak guard disqualifies any stem or option that mentions stitching, panoramas, yaw, or file paths. The directionmetadata consistency check parses the answer text of verifiable templates (camera rotation, translation, photographer-relative direction) for direction keywords and compares them against yaw and pitch: yaw shifts above 3 require horizontal direction with the correct sign and reject answers that are purely vertical, and pitch shifts work analogously. Uniqueness grounding sends every named noun phrase from the questions back to the model in separate call asking it to count visible candidate matches in its image, and only objects flagged as uniquely present survive; we found object naming from single forward pass to be the largest source of unverifiable references. Finally, reverse-solve gate re-runs each question blind against fresh model call with the exact images and options under prompt that requires explicit object localization, angular and depth judgment, 8-direction classification, and option matching, and items where the reverse-solver disagrees with the generator are dropped. Step 4: Post-processing. After CoT generation we apply conservative line-by-line filter as final defense against CoT-level inconsistencies that the per-question gates in Step 3 cannot see. The filter drops rows whose reasoning chain contradicts the rotation direction encoded in the gold option, whose CoT is empty or under twenty whitespace tokens, or whose gold letter does not extract to non-empty option text in the prompt. Birds-eye view synthesis. The next departure leaves the input agents position altogether and synthesizes world-anchored overhead view. Source scenes come from Mindcube [106]. An overhead view makes object positions, distances, and ego-relative directions directly readable, so the model can consult it as an intermediate image during reasoning. To be usable as visual thought, the synthesized map must be geometrically faithful so that the original answer survives the view substitution, stable under sparse-view inputs, and realistic enough that unified VLM treats it as photograph rather than diagram. To our knowledge no public tool produces sparse-view top-down image of an indoor scene under these constraints. We tried three natural candidates from adjacent fields, summarized in Table 8 and illustrated in Figure 9. Candidates that are strong on appearance tend to be weak on geometric consistency, and candidates that are strong on geometry produce outputs that do not look photographic. We split the problem along that boundary. reconstruction stage commits to where objects are and how they are oriented relative to horizontal support plane, and generative stage paints that layout to look photographic. The minimizer q0 is the approximate point of common visual focus. When camera poses are missing we fall back to the confidenceweighted centroid of the cloud. To separate foreground from background, we sort point distances to q0 and look for the first large gap relative to the median adjacent difference. The radius before that gap is taken as the foreground extent and the rest is discarded as distant background. We then refine the center to the confidence-weighted mean over the foreground subset and set to fixed percentile of distances from to the refined center. Using percentile rather than the maximum keeps framing stable across scenes by ignoring the tail of weakly reconstructed points. Step 3: Overhead camera frame. We recover the top-down direction by fitting the dominant horizontal plane to the cloud with RANSAC (PCA fallback on degenerate clouds). When camera 29 poses are available we sharpen the fit with two pose-aware constraints: the candidate normal must roughly align with the average camera up direction, and most camera centers must lie on the same side of the plane. Together these push the fit toward the actual support surface and reject vertical structures such as walls. The normals sign is resolved by flipping it toward the side that contains more cameras. We align its right axis with the reference camera when one is available, so all rendered top-downs share consistent orientation across scenes; otherwise we derive the right axis from canonical world up vector. Camera intrinsics are standard pinhole, with the field of view widened on square outputs to avoid clipping the source aspect ratio. Step 4: Rendering and photographic texturing. We project the surviving points into the overhead camera using standard pinhole projection, drop points behind the camera, and resolve per-pixel collisions by keeping the nearest hit. The result is geometrically faithful but visually sparse, so it serves as structural conditioning rather than as the final image. As cheap consistency check, we also render the point cloud from the original reference camera pose and discard the scene if the cloud and the pose disagree there, before paying the cost of texturing. LoRA-fine-tuned Qwen-Image-Edit-2511 [91] turns the sparse rendering into photographic top-down. We feed the sparse rendering as the image-conditioning input and train the LoRA [36] to reproduce real overhead photograph of the same scene. Egoexo perspective transfer (Ego-Exo4D). Ego-Exo4D [29] records every activity simultaneously with head-mounted Aria camera and several stationary GoPro cameras, so the photographers first-person view is paired frame-for-frame with several third-person views of the same scene. Given third-person photograph in which the photographer is visible, the answer to what is to your left from this persons perspective? reduces to direct ego-frame fact. We convert each Ego-Exo4D take into multiple-choice perspective-taking questions. The third-person image is the models input, and the photographers ego frame is attached as reasoning aid. The third-person image used as input is unmarked. We do draw green marker on the photographers projected head, but only on parallel copy of the same exo frame, kept in metadata for reviewer inspection. Marking the input would let any model identify the photographer trivially from color and bypass the perspective-taking signal. The pipeline runs in three steps. First, per-take nine-pack exports three ego frames, three exo frames, and three exo-marked frames. Then two-stage GPT pipeline writes one or two perspective-taking 30 questions per frame. deterministic post-processor then selects balanced subset across takes and answer axes. 4 Step 1: Nine-pack construction. For every take we select three ego frames that jointly maximize in-focus quality and visual diversity. Per-frame sharpness is the variance of the Laplacian on central 3 4 crop of the rectified ego frame. Using the per-take time synchronization, we map each ego-frame index to trajectory time and read the device world position pworld off the closed-loop trajectory. We then transform pworld into the exo camera frame as pcam = Rcam,world(pworld tworld,cam) with the GoPro extrinsics, and project it through the Kannala Brandt fisheye model. Writing pcam = (x, y, z), the model maps it to image coordinates (u, v) through = x/z, = y/z, = (cid:112) a2 + b2, θ = arctan r, θd = θ + k0θ3 + k1θ5 + k2θ7 + k3θ9, (u, v) = (cid:0)fx (θd/r) + cx, fy (θd/r) + cy (cid:1), where (fx, fy), (cx, cy), and {k0, . . . , k3} are the per-camera intrinsics. point projects to marker only when it lies in front of the camera (z > 0) and (u, v) falls inside the exo frame. Otherwise no marker is drawn and the frame is exported with the marker layer suppressed. Takes with missing or invalid timesync, trajectory, or calibration files are skipped by default. Step 2: Two-stage VQA generation. From each frame in the nine-pack we generate up to two perspective-taking questions. The single-object axis question picks one visible object near single edge of the photographers view, with the answer drawn from {left, right, above, below}. The object-pair relation question picks target and reference, with the answer drawn from {left, right, above, below, front, behind}. Both branches use two-stage GPT pipeline that routes images so that the spatial fact and the question wording are decided in different stages from different views. In the candidate stage the model sees only the ego image and proposes the spatial fact: target object (and, for the pair branch, reference) plus the chosen direction label. Question wording is forbidden at this stage. In the finalize stage the model sees only the exo image with the marker on the photographer and rewrites the candidate fact into perspective-taking question, naming the photographer naturally by clothing, role, or position, picking an opener from small bank of templates, and forcing the either-or option form. The finalize stage never sees the ego image, so it cannot redo the spatial reasoning, only re-phrase it. This split removes two failure modes we saw when single prompt did both: the model invented spatial answers to match the marker rather than the ego frame, and the question stem leaked the answer through phrases like the person is on the left, so must be on his left. With the split, the spatial fact is fixed by the candidate stage and the finalize stage is constrained to keep the same target and chosen axis. Each candidates chosen axis fixes binary either-or option pair (left/right, above/below, or front/behind), which determines the gold letter directly. Step 3: Balanced subset selection. The raw corpus is naturally imbalanced. Single-object axis questions skew toward whichever direction the activity faces in each take, and some takes contribute many more frames than others. deterministic post-processor produces balanced subset by greedy selection. We first reduce to at most one row per (take, frame) by random selection between the single-object and pair candidates of the same frame, so no frame contributes twice. We then pick rows in two phases. Phase 1 walks the takes in shuffled order and adds, from each take, the row whose addition 31 would most reduce the imbalance across the three axis pairs (left vs. right, above vs. below, front vs. behind), with under-represented pair totals and smaller absolute counts as tie-breakers. This yields at most one row per take in an order that keeps the answer distribution close to per-axis balanced. If the target subset size is larger than the number of distinct takes, Phase 2 pulls from the remaining pool with the same scoring rule but without the per-take constraint. The end result is subset with near 50/50 splits on each axis pair and maximally diverse take base for the requested size. Alternate-view rendering (SAM3D). When only single image is available, we cannot rely on paired second camera. Instead we lift the image to 3D, pick any directional entity in the scene (a person, chair, TV) as the viewer, and render the rest of the scene from the viewers inferred pose. The supervision target is question like from the chairs point of view, is the lamp to the left or right of the table?. Every gold answer is computed analytically from 3D vector geometry. The language model, when invoked at all, only plays validator and natural-language polisher. The construction emits three layered reasoning images per question: who-is-who image showing role-colored masks on the original image, an orientation image showing the viewers basis pasted at the viewers centroid, and the viewer-perspective render with the viewer hidden. model trained to consume them works through them as an interleaved visual chain of thought during reasoning. The pipeline runs in four steps. Before describing them we note the front-end choice. Detection and segmentation front end. Before settling on RAM++ [116], SAM3 [7], and SAM3D-Objects [67] we tried several alternatives. Combining RAM++ with Grounding DINO or Florence-2 produced boxes that were too loose for clean single-object splats. SAM3 alone gave high mask quality when it fired, but recall was too low: many RAM++ tags never produced usable instance, which blocked triplet discovery. hybrid that piped RAM++ through WeDetect into SAM3 improved coverage somewhat, but WeDetect boxes were often clipped at the object boundary, and those truncated masks propagated into incomplete 3D geometry. The RAM++ SAM3 OriAnyV2 [88] stack we ship traded small loss in vocabulary recall for tighter masks and reliable orientation, which matters more for downstream rendering. Step 1: 2D perception. For each input image we run RAM++ to produce list of open-vocabulary tags, then call SAM3 once per tag with the tag as the segmentation prompt to obtain per-instance masks at the original image resolution. tag-aware non-maximum suppression removes both within-tag duplicates (a single chair detected many times) and tag-internal hierarchical duplicates (a sofa mask containing its cushions). Any mask whose bounding box covers more than 60% of the image is dropped, since these are almost always background panels (walls, floors, sky) that the tagger picked up. For every surviving instance we predict its 3D orientation with OriAnyV2, which returns the objects canonical-front azimuth, elevation, and roll relative to the camera frame, together with binary directional-front flag. Only instances flagged as directional (TVs, sofas, beds) can serve as viewers whose forward direction is read off the predicted orientation; non-directional instances (spheres, bowls, lamps) either play the target role or, if used as the viewer, fall back to look-toward-the-targets view direction. Step 2: Per-instance 3D reconstruction. Each (image, instance mask) pair is reconstructed independently into 3D Gaussian splat by SAM3D-Objects. For this branch of the corpus we use MS COCO 2017 [51] (train and val splits) as the only image source, so reconstruction statistics stay tied to single domain. The model outputs per-object Gaussian set in local frame together with rigid-plus-isotropic transform (R, t, s) that takes the object into shared canonical frame. We compose multiple objects into scene by applying these transforms to the per-Gaussian centers, rotating each Gaussians covariance quaternion accordingly, and concatenating the Gaussian buffers. Per-object scales are clamped to be at least 1.1 the merged kernel size to absorb mild scale inconsistency between independent reconstructions. After composition we apply fixed axis-swap to align the scene with +Y -up convention and re-normalize so the active Gaussians largest extent is unit length. Reconstructing per-instance rather than fitting whole scene at once keeps each splat small and decouples reconstruction failures across unrelated regions, at the cost of mild per-object scale drift that the clamping and re-normalization absorb. Step 3: Viewer-perspective rendering. For each candidate viewertarget triplet (one viewer plus the two targets that will appear in the question) we place virtual camera at the viewers center, looking along the viewers forward direction, and render the remaining objects through 32 that camera. For directional viewers the forward direction is the negative of the first column of the predicted orientation matrix (the camera looks out of the objects front); for non-directional viewers it is look-at vector toward the centroid of the targets. We jointly fit the camera position and field of view so that the targets fit with small margin and the viewer does not clip the camera. small ladder of backoff distances (multiples of the scene diagonal) and angular widths is swept, and we accept the smallest pair (backoff, fov) for which every target AABB corner = ccam satisfies atan2(cid:0)v r, (cid:1) < fov/2 and > 0, where is the camera forward axis and = its right axis built from the global up vector. The smallest fitting pair preserves the illusion that the camera sits at the viewer object. Larger backoffs and wider angular extents are only allowed when no smaller pair fits. We hide the viewer in the render by zeroing the opacity of its Gaussians, so the viewer disappears from the image while the rest of the buffer stays intact. Two sanity checks finalize the candidate. Each targets AABB must project to non-empty bounding box in the rendered view (i.e., lie in front of the camera and inside the image), and the two target bboxes must not overlap in render coordinates, since overlap means the question is not visually answerable from the render alone. Candidates failing either check are dropped. Step 4: Question synthesis. For each accepted candidate we emit one or two multiple-choice questions from small set of deterministic templates. The current templates ask (i) whether one target is to the left or right of the other from the viewers standpoint, and (ii) which of the two targets the viewer is facing more toward. Both gold answers are computed analytically from the camera basis (f , r) and the relative vectors relX = cX cviewer. For the left/right question we project each targets offset onto the viewers right axis, xa = rela r, xb = relb r, and pick left iff xa < xb, subject to minimum normalized margin xa xb/(rela + relb) δLR so close-call configurations are rejected. For the facing question we measure each targets angular offset from the viewers forward axis, angleX = arccos(cid:0)(relX )/relX (cid:1), and pick whichever target has the smaller angle, subject to minimum angular margin between the two angles. Rejecting close-call candidates makes the gold answers safe to use as supervision, since small reconstruction error nudging the two targets in opposite directions cannot silently flip the answer. vision-language model is invoked twice, optionally. It can validate candidate by viewing the three reasoning artefacts produced in Step 3 and either accepting it or rejecting it as visually ambiguous, under system prompt that asks for conservative rejection. It can also polish the question stem into more natural language while the gold answer and option pair stay frozen. The model is never given authority over the answer. Object phrasings in the stem are disambiguated automatically. Viewer choice is restricted to instances the stem can refer to unambiguously, which means singletons of their tag, instances with unique color within their tag group, or strictly leftmost or rightmost in bbox order. When multiple instances of the same tag remain, the chosen one is referred to as left, right, leftmost, rightmost, or middle by its centroid-x rank within the group. The stem therefore stays unambiguous even when several chairs sit in the same scene. D.4.2 Object manipulation The remaining family of mental world modeling keeps the camera fixed and transforms the object itself. We supervise the simplest case: rigid rotation of the object about vertical axis, which the model must imagine and produce as second view of the same object from another angle. Object rotation (Viewpoint-100K). The model is given one image of an object and the supervision target is second view of the same object after horizontal rotation, with mostly the same subject framing. The supervision comes from Viewpoint-100K [111], which provides one hundred thousand calibrated pairs of multi-view frames of the same physical object, built from MVImgNet [108] (roughly 6.5M real multi-view frames with object masks, intrinsics, extrinsics, depth, and point clouds per subject). For each sample, two views of the same instance are drawn with horizontal separation between 20 and 100, over 10,813 distinct object identities across 205 classes. 33 We repackage those pairs as edit-the-input examples. The first frame is the image to be transformed, the second is the supervision target or auxiliary visual thought, and the text prompt describes the relative rotation in natural language rather than exposing raw calibration tuples. The geometric relationship between the pair is unchanged from the public release; only the prompt and field layout are adapted to our trace format. sections.title: G Training and Evaluation Details
sections.content: This section documents the training and evaluation setup. The training configuration below produces the ThinkMorph-SSL checkpoint reported in Section 4.3. Both stages fine-tune the same BAGEL-7BMoT backbone [17] under FSDP2 sharding with the in-house bagel_fsdp2_trainer; what differs across stages is the data, the training horizon, the world size, and few token-budget parameters. Table 10 summarises every hyperparameter. The loss and the verbatim system prompt follow it, compute and runtime numbers are in Table 12, and Section G.2 describes the evaluation. G.1 Training Per-stage hyperparameters. Table 10 lists every hyperparameter that differs between Stage 1 (pretext reasoning) and Stage 2 (instruction tuning) alongside the few that are shared. Stage 1 trains Pretext-270K from the BAGEL-7B-MoT checkpoint released by [17] on 32 GPUs across 4 nodes; Stage 2 resumes from the Stage 1 EMA checkpoint at step 5500 on 48 GPUs across 6 nodes. The 2 scaling of 2e-5 base when moving from 16-GPU pilot to the Stage 1 learning rate is the production 32-GPU run; Stage 2 reverts to the unscaled 2e-5. The per-device batch size is fixed at 1 with gradient accumulation 1, so the effective batch size is the world size (32 in Stage 1, 48 in Stage 2). We rely on dynamic sequence packing up to max_num_tokens (16,384 in Stage 1, 20,480 in Stage 2) instead of micro-batching, which keeps per-step throughput high under the heterogeneous trace lengths of Instruct-180K. Ablation runs. The BAGEL-7B ablations in Section 4.4 use the trainer and loss above. Table 11 lists the settings that differ from Table 10. Full training data. The Stage-2-only run trains Instruct-180K from BAGEL-7B-MoT with the Stage-2 settings of Table 10 on 32 GPUs. The staged run is the main Stage-2 run on 48 GPUs. We compare the Stage-2-only EMA checkpoint at step 3,000 with the staged EMA checkpoint at step 2,000, so both runs have taken about 100K Stage-2 sequences (steps world size). Spatial training subset. All runs use 8 GPUs with per-device batch size 1, so the effective batch size is 8, and no EMA. Stage 1 trains on 50K pretext traces built from the images of the spatial training subset for 10,000 steps. Stage 2 trains on the spatial training subset of Instruct-180K from the Stage-1 checkpoint at step 10,000, and we evaluate every 2,000 steps; the figures call each such interval Stage-2 epoch. The one-stage run trains on both sets together and samples them in proportion to their size. The instructed variant differs from the staged run only in the Stage-1 inputs. InternVL-U-4B uses the same settings as BAGEL-7B. Loss and optimisation. The training objective sums cross-entropy term on text tokens and mean-squared-error term on the VAE latents that the image-generation head produces; both terms are evaluated at every interleaved trace position the processor labels as supervised. We never freeze the image-generation pathway: at Pretext-270K time the VAE-MSE term teaches the model to reproduce the restored image, and at Instruct-180K time it teaches the model to generate intermediate visual states that the subsequent thoughts can attend to. The VAE encoder itself (vae_model) is frozen across both stages so the latent space stays fixed. Both loss terms have weight 1.0, and both stages use the same processor and conditional-dropout settings. System prompt and special tokens. Both stages share an identical action-control system prompt that declares the three special tokens (<think>, <gen_image>, <answer>) and the inline imagesize syntax. We set wrap_assistant_reasoning_with_think=true so every reasoning span is wrapped in <think>...</think> before any image is emitted, which keeps the trace machineparseable even when the model emits multiple image-thought rounds. The box below reproduces the prompt verbatim. Action-control system prompt (verbatim, identical across Stage 1 and Stage 2) Use <think>...</think> for intermediate reasoning or planning. We document the evaluation framework, the per-benchmark scoring protocols, and the LLM-judge configuration used to produce all reported numbers. We evaluate inside fork of VLMEvalKit that adds the patches required for our interleaved (text+image) generation interface, plus the dataset modules for the spatial benchmarks that are not yet upstream (MMSI, MINDCUBE, OMNISPATIAL, SPATIALVIZ-BENCH).
