The judge uses one prompt template for every benchmark. It is asked to do two things in one call: (i) extract normalized final answer from the candidate trace, and (ii) grade that extracted answer against the gold answer as one of A=correct, B=incorrect, C=invalid. The prompt is reproduced verbatim in the box below. The output format is single line <GRADE>t<EXTRACTED_ANSWER>; we parse the first non-empty line of the response to recover both fields. Judge prompt (verbatim) used for MMSI fallback and OmniSpatial You are an expert grading assistant. Your job has TWO tasks: 1) From the candidates full response, EXTRACT the final answer in concise, normalized form. 2) Compare this extracted answer with the STANDARD ANSWER and grade it as: - A: CORRECT - B: INCORRECT - C: INVALID Here are the detailed evaluation criteria: 1. ALWAYS refer to the given STANDARD ANSWER. You do NOT need to re-solve the question; the standard answer has already been provided and is always correct. Your only job is to judge whether the candidates final answer is consistent with the standard answer according to the form of the question. THE STANDARD ANSWER IS ALWAYS CORRECT AND THE QUESTION IS PERFECTLY VALID. NEVER QUESTION THEM. 2. ONLY compare the FINAL ANSWER -- COMPLETELY IGNORE any potential errors or issues in the REASONING PROCESS. Even if the reasoning is wrong, as long as the final answer matches the standard answer, grade it as CORRECT. 3. Answers may be expressed in different ways (e.g., mathematical expressions, textual descriptions). As long as the meaning is the same as the standard answer, treat them as equivalent. If the standard answer does not specify unit but the candidates answer includes correct unit for the given value, consider it CORRECT. 4. Some answers may consist of multiple items, such as multiple-choice questions with multiple correct options, multi-select questions, or multi-blank fill-in-the-blank questions. Regardless of the question type, the final answer is considered CORRECT only if it matches the standard answer exactly at the level of all required items. For multi-select or multi-blank questions, ALL parts must be answered correctly and match the standard answer exactly to be deemed CORRECT. 5. If the candidates answer is wrapped in LaTeX-style markers like boxed{...}, IGNORE the boxed and only use the inner content as the candidates final answer when comparing with the standard answer. 6. If the candidates answer is INVALID -- for example, incomplete (cut off mid-response), containing large amount of abnormal repetitive content, clearly irrelevant to the question, or explicitly refusing to answer due to ethical concerns, lack of information, or other external factors -- then you MUST grade it as C: INVALID. 7. This instruction applies to all problem types, including single-choice MCQ, multi-select MCQ, numeric problems, short-answer questions, and general VQA-style questions. In all cases, only the FINAL ANSWER and its consistency with the standard answer matter. 8. The question or options may contain image placeholders such as <image>, <image id=1>, or similar tokens. You CANNOT see these images. Treat these placeholders as unknown content and DO NOT hallucinate or infer any specific visual details from them. If the standard answer or candidates answer refers to an option associated with an image (e.g., choose A), judge correctness only based on the stated answer, not by imagining the image. 53 IMPORTANT -- OUTPUT FORMAT: * You MUST return EXACTLY ONE line in the following format: <GRADE>t<EXTRACTED_ANSWER> where <GRADE> is one of A, B, or C. * <EXTRACTED_ANSWER> should be the final answer you extracted from the candidates response, in normalized, concise form (e.g., number, letter option, or short phrase). * If you cannot extract any meaningful answer, or the response is INVALID, output: CtN/A * Do NOT add any extra text, explanation, or additional lines. Now, judge the following question. <Original Question Begin> {question} {options_block} <Original Question End> <Standard Answer Begin> {gold_answer} <Standard Answer End> <Candidates Answer Begin> {llm_response} <Candidates Answer End> Your output: Per-benchmark customization. For MCQ benchmarks the judge sees the option block formatted as Options:n A. ...n B. ...; the gold answer is rewritten as <letter>. <option text> so that the judge can recover from cases where the candidate writes only the option text without the letter. For free-form (VQA-mode) benchmarks the option block is empty and the gold answer is passed through verbatim. The gradescore mapping is A1, B0, C0, with the count separately reported as the invalid rate so that overall accuracy and accuracy-among-valid can both be recovered.

sections.title: H Additional Analyses
sections.content: This section presents qualitative cases, discusses overlap between our training data and the evaluation benchmarks, and covers alternative routes without visual-state training. Evaluations follow the protocol in Section G.2. H.1 Qualitative cases Here we show six reasoning traces from the evaluation: three where ThinkMorph-SSL answers correctly (Figures 10 to 12) and three where it does not (Figures 13 to 15). Every card lays the input scene, the question, the parsed answers from Qwen2.5-VL-7B and BAGEL-7B-MoT (think-4k) on the same prompt, and ThinkMorph-SSLs full <think>[Generated Image: ...]<think> trace ending in parsed answer letter. The intermediate image changes with the level of the question. On L1, the model renders focused view of the queried region; on L2, it emits spatial aid such as depth map or the objects to count, masked out; on L3, it constructs scene state that the input does not show, such as top-down map or shifted viewpoint on MindCube and merged panorama on MMSI. The cases share high-level pattern: ThinkMorph-SSLs intermediate image is purpose-built visual scaffold that converts the question into read-off step. When the scaffold matches an operator the Instruct-180K curriculum has trained (Section D) and is correctly instantiated, ThinkMorph-SSL outperforms both 7B-class baselines. When the scaffold is the wrong tool, the trace can still be locally coherent but lands on the wrong answer. Good cases: what the intermediate image is doing. The three success traces use two distinct intermediate-image roles. Depth views answer relative-distance questions. Figures 10 and 11 show CV-Bench-3D prompts that compare the real-world distances of three boxed objects. ThinkMorph-SSL renders viridis depth map and reads the answer off the colour bands. Crops disambiguate counts in cluttered scenes. Figure 12 asks how many people are seated at café table next to standing distractor. From the global view both baselines say two. ThinkMorphSSL crops to the table and counts only the seated bodies, arriving at three. In all three cases the heavy lifting sits in the rendered image; the surrounding text reasoning is short. Failure modes. The three failures split into two qualitatively different kinds: one out-of-distribution case, where the question is far from anything Instruct-180K trains and ThinkMorph-SSL has no scaffold that fits, and two in-distribution mistakes, where the right kind of intermediate image is in scope but the rendered version is noisy or incomplete. Out-of-distribution: no useful intermediate to render. Figure 13 asks which of four cube nets, when folded, cannot reproduce shown cube question about face adjacencies under unfolding. ThinkMorph-SSL has not seen anything like it during training. It still emits generated image, but the rendered view simply colors every view blue, so the second thought reasons over depth-coded adjacency that has nothing to do with the topology of the question and arrives at the wrong answer. Both baselines reach the right answer by language-only reasoning. Noisy intermediate. The rendered intermediates in the next two cases are themselves wrong, and the read-back steps inherit their mistakes. Figure 14 asks for the number of cars in festival scene. ThinkMorph-SSL announces mask-overlay intermediate to isolate only the cars, but the rendered mask highlights person carrying an umbrella instead of any of the vehicles. The second thought reads back from that wrong mask and the parsed answer is wrong, even though the question is well within Instruct-180Ks scope. Figure 15 states cardinal constraint in text (chandelier is north of the stove) and asks what lies east of the dining room. ThinkMorph-SSL chooses the right kind of intermediate (a panorama merge of the two ego frames), but the rendered panorama is essentially Input 1 duplicated it does not actually splice information from Input 2 into single continuous layout. The second thought 55 Figure 10: CV-Bench-3D: depth map shows the bookcase shares the back-wall band with the desk while the books sit in the foreground. reasons over degenerate panorama and picks the wrong east object; Qwen2.5-VL-7B reaches the gold answer with no intermediate image at all. Figure 11: CV-Bench-3D: same depth scaffold on rainy street; the truck and pedestrian fall in the same far band while the car is closer. 57 Figure 12: HRBench-4k: tight crop separates seated diners from standing distractor. 58 Figure 13: SpatialViz-Bench (out-of-distribution): the rendered intermediate is near-uniform blue image with no usable structure, so the second thought has nothing to read back from. Figure 14: CV-Bench-2D mistake: the model declares car-segmentation mask but the rendered overlay highlights person carrying an umbrella; the read-back step then reasons about the wrong objects. 60 Figure 15: MMSI mistake: the rendered panorama is essentially Input 1 duplicated rather than real merge of the two ego views, so the layout the second thought reads is incomplete. 61 H.2 Data overlap and contamination BAGELs pretraining data are not public, so we cannot measure image-level overlap between our source images and its pretraining corpus, and we do not claim that every source image in Pretext-270K is unseen. Possible overlap in raw images does not, however, make Stage 1 lookup task. Each Stage-1 trace presents newly corrupted or transformed input, and the model must infer what changed, generate the restored image, and continue the trace. The corruptions, trace format, and descriptions are constructed by our pipeline, so even an image seen during pretraining did not appear in this form. On the evaluation side, Instruct-180K does not reuse benchmark questions or official templates, and all benchmarks are evaluated on held-out test splits. These measures rule out training on evaluation questions and prior exposure to our exact traces, but not every effect of overlap in pretraining images. H.3 Alternative routes without visual-state training Text-only fine-tuning could in principle give unified model visual reasoning without training it to generate and use intermediate images. Prompting alone does not suffice, as shown in Table 2. Text-only reasoning fine-tuning. ThinkMorph [30] fine-tunes BAGEL-7B on the same training problems with either text-only or interleaved traces, so the data are fixed and only the reasoning mode changes. Text-only traces raise out-of-domain accuracy from 55.49 to 56.02 on V, from 67.33 to 68.67 on BLINK-Jigsaw, and from 70.33 to 76.33 on MMVP; interleaved traces reach 63.87, 73.33, and 82.66. With the data held fixed, the larger gain comes with constructing visual state, not with reasoning fine-tuning as such.
